empathy

/EM-puh-thee/ - the stress falls on EM · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Empathy means the ability to understand and share another person's feelings.

Good referees need empathy as much as rulebooks, sensing when a rattled young player needs a quiet word instead of a card.

Example

When layoffs hit the plant, the shift supervisor showed an empathy the executives lacked: she had run the same machines for years, and workers said she seemed to carry each lost job as if the notice had her own name on it.

Empathy is stronger and more specific than sympathy or pity: sympathy feels for someone from the outside, and pity can even look down on them, but empathy climbs inside — understanding and sharing the feeling as if it were your own.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

understanding: Understanding is grasping someone's situation — you can understand a decision coldly, from the facts alone. Empathy requires feeling: not just mapping what happened to a person but sharing the emotion itself as if it were yours.

pity: Pity is sorrow for someone seen as worse off, and it often looks down from above. Empathy allows no looking down: it climbs inside the other person's position and shares the feeling as an equal.

sensitivity: Sensitivity is alertness to other people's feelings — noticing the wince, reading the room. Empathy goes a step further inward: beyond detecting a feeling, it means actually sharing it, carrying another's trouble as your own.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

indifference: not caring either way

callousness: hardened lack of feeling for others

Where it sits · how deeply another's trouble is taken on — sympathy → empathy → compassion

sympathy vs. empathy: Sympathy stands beside the sufferer and feels sorry for them; it stops short of empathy, which crosses over and feels the trouble from the inside.

compassion vs. empathy: Compassion goes a step further than empathy: it takes the shared feeling and turns it into the urge to help.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — em-

Prefix — em-: in, within (a form of en-)

Root — path

Root — path: feeling, suffering (Greek pathos)

Suffix — -y

Suffix — -y: noun-forming: a state or quality

Put it together

Put it together: Greek pathos means 'feeling, suffering'; em- puts you in it; -y wraps the whole thing into a noun. Empathy is literally 'in-feeling' — the state of being inside another person's emotion. The word is young in English: psychologists coined it around 1900 to translate German Einfühlung, 'feeling-into.'

Use the root in a new word: apathy

Use the root in a new word: apathy: The op-ed blamed apathy for Tuesday's result.

Word Choice

neutral

Empathy is the precise choice when you mean feeling a thing from inside someone else's position. Sympathy is warmer but stays outside; compassion adds the impulse to help. SAT passages about narrators and characters often turn on exactly this distinction, so keep the three apart.
